Lessons.Title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: add or subtract two linear equations with opposite/equal coefficients to eliminate a variable, solve the remaining equation and connect the pair to the graphs' common intersection. Edulytiks independent adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L14, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/14/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Addressing HSA-REI.C.6; Building Towards HSA-REI.C.5.

Original balanced-relationship example: x+y=13 and x−y=3. Adding both equations yields 2x=16 (the +y and −y cancel), giving x=8 and y=5. The sum line 2x=16 passes through the same intersection as both original lines, but it is not by itself equivalent to the entire original system.

Elimination is appropriate when one variable has equal or opposite coefficients. For 3a+2b=18 and 3a−2b=6, adding yields 6a=24 -> a=4, then b=3. A second strategy subtracts if coefficients are identical rather than opposites.

Student task: make an original visual balance diagram or equivalent text table, add/subtract two equations, graph both originals and their sum, describe the single shared intersection and justify why it survives the operation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct operation, cancellation, back-substitution and graph/argument; group-created diagrams are not single-number auto-grades.

KeyConcepts.Title: Elimination
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine full equations to cancel a variable by equal/opposite coefficients.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add equations term-by-term or subtract the entire equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: A system solution satisfies any sum of its true equalities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both originals, not just the newly summed equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph intersection
KeyConcepts.Definition: A third equation formed by adding has a line containing the original intersection.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Don't confuse one combined equation with a replacement for both constraints.
KeyConcepts.Example: The line x=8 also passes through (8,5).

WorkedExamples.Title: Eliminate opposite coefficients
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve x+y=13 and x−y=3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each mathematical move and verify the result in the original equations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Eliminate in two more-variable equations
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve 3a+2b=18 and 3a−2b=6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each mathematical move and verify the result in the original equations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish sum line from full system
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (8,0) solve 2x=16 and both original equations x+y=13,x−y=3?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain each mathematical move and verify the result in the original equations.
Steps: Thus one new equation has extra solutions; retain an original constraint.
WorkedExamples.Answer: (8,0) solves the combined equation but not the original system.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Combining coefficients without combining full right sides
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The sum must operate on both sides.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add both left sides and both right sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the sum line equals the full system
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use remaining original equation to determine the actual pair.

SummaryPoints: Opposite coefficients allow a variable to disappear when equations are added.
The original system intersection is on the sum line.
For x+y=13 and x−y=3, the shared solution is (8,5).
Explain the graph connection rather than only giving a pair.
